ocar.opportunity: When a serial-EM sample is rare or imaging conditions drift, the goal is to label the stack in hand, not to generalize to future volumes.
ocar.challenge: Standard supervised segmentation assumes enough labels and a generalization target; that is the wrong setting for small, unique series.
ocar.action: Takaya, Takeichi, Ozaki, and Kurihara, in Journal of Neuroscience Methods (2021), propose sequential semi-supervised segmentation (4S): iterate train–infer–pseudo-label along the series, exploiting correlation between adjacent sections, from few teacher labels.
ocar.resolution: On two serial-section image types the abstract reports qualitative and quantitative gains versus supervised learning with few labels, and it examines how the number and position of teacher labels affect performance. The method is framed as a transductive extractor of neural regions from EM stacks.
ocar.future_work: The authors planned to embed 4S in a general-purpose annotation tool.

summaries.beginner: If you only labeled a few slices in a stack of electron-microscope pictures, you still want the rest filled in. This methods paper walks a network along the stack, using each slice to help the next, instead of pretending it must work on brand-new samples.
summaries.intermediate: Takaya, Takeichi, Ozaki, and Kurihara (Journal of Neuroscience Methods, 2021) introduce sequential semi-supervised segmentation (4S) for serial EM. The setting is transductive: predict all labels in a given stack from partial labels, using adjacent-slice correlation and iterative pseudo-labeling. Experiments on two serial-image types are said to beat few-label supervised learning, with an ablation on teacher-label number and placement.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not name the two image types, report numeric scores, or specify how many teacher labels were used. Independent reading of the Journal of Neuroscience Methods paper is required for datasets and metrics.

plain_language_summary: If you only labeled a few slices in a stack of electron-microscope pictures, you still want the rest filled in. This methods paper walks a network along the stack, using each slice to help the next, instead of pretending it must work on brand-new samples.

ocar.opportunity: Resting-state fMRI connectivity can define a robust endophenotype in Fmr1-/y mice, a Fragile X model, and would be more useful if it could also detect circuit-level effects of drugs.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown whether this macroscopic connectivity measure is sensitive enough to pick up pharmacological rescue, and whether any rescue would track behavior and white-matter structure.
ocar.action: Zerbi, Markicevic, Gasparini, Schroeter, Rudin, and Wenderoth, in NeuroImage (2019), inhibited mGluR5 with AFQ056/Mavoglurant and used rs-fMRI plus diffusion-weighted imaging in Fmr1-/y mice, focusing on circuits related to social behavior.
ocar.resolution: Fmr1-/y mice showed impaired social interaction, reduced connectivity in three main functional networks, and altered network topology. At group level, Mavoglurant rescued neither abnormal social behavior nor white-matter abnormalities, but it had a genotype-specific effect of restoring functional connectivity in some, not all, of those circuits.
ocar.future_work: The abstract concludes that rs-fMRI connectivity can detect system-level mGluR5 inhibition, but effects are circuit-confined, so behavioral benefits may be restricted to narrow functional domains.

summaries.beginner: A mouse model of Fragile X has odd brain-network coupling on MRI. This study asks whether an mGluR5 drug puts those networks back, and finds that some circuits improve on the scan even when social behavior and white matter do not.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2019), Zerbi and colleagues test whether Mavoglurant (AFQ056), an mGluR5 inhibitor, restores connectivity in Fmr1-/y mice. Using rs-fMRI and DWI, they replicate impaired social interaction, reduced connectivity in three main functional networks, and altered topology. Group-level Mavoglurant did not rescue social behavior or white-matter abnormalities, but restored functional connectivity in a genotype-specific way in some affected circuits. The abstract treats rs-fMRI as sensitive to pharmacological change yet spatially limited.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Sample sizes, named networks, and DWI metrics are not in the abstract. Catalog organism is untagged; the abstract is mouse Fragile X.

plain_language_summary: A mouse model of Fragile X has odd brain-network coupling on MRI. This study asks whether an mGluR5 drug puts those networks back, and finds that some circuits improve on the scan even when social behavior and white matter do not.

ocar.opportunity: In sensory cortex, intermingled neurons encode different stimulus attributes and send them to different long-range targets; knowing whether those output channels also keep separate local synapses would explain how parallel streams stay independent.
ocar.challenge: Like-to-like connectivity based on sensory responses is established, but the relationship between within-area synapses and long-range projection target was unclear.
ocar.action: Kim, Znamenskiy, Iacaruso, and Mrsic-Flogel, in Neuron (2018), examined local connectivity and visual responses of mouse primary visual cortex neurons that project to anterolateral (AL) versus posteromedial (PM) higher visual areas.
ocar.resolution: Layer 2/3 neurons projecting to different targets often had similar visual responses but avoided connecting with each other. Projection target, in addition to response similarity, therefore constrains local synaptic connectivity of AL and PM projection neurons. The authors propose that reduced crosstalk permits independent function of these output channels.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the independence of output channels as an interpretation of the avoided connections; further tests of function across areas are not specified in the catalog abstract.

summaries.beginner: Cells in visual cortex that send axons to different next-stage areas often see the world similarly. This paper finds they still avoid linking to each other locally, which may keep those output pipelines from mixing.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2018), Kim, Znamenskiy, Iacaruso, and Mrsic-Flogel map local connectivity and visual responses of mouse V1 neurons projecting to AL versus PM. Despite often-similar responses, L2/3 AL- and PM-projecting cells avoided synapses with each other. The authors conclude that projection target constrains local connectivity beyond response similarity and propose that this reduced crosstalk supports independent output channels.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Connection probabilities, cell counts, and recording methods are not in the abstract. Catalog organism is untagged; the abstract is mouse V1.

plain_language_summary: Cells in visual cortex that send axons to different next-stage areas often see the world similarly. This paper finds they still avoid linking to each other locally, which may keep those output pipelines from mixing.

ocar.opportunity: Without a unifying mathematical framework, it is hard to describe how a neural network’s structure determines its emergent function, including how cortex processes information.
ocar.challenge: Graph-theoretic analyses usually ignore the direction of synaptic transmission and stay at local connectivity, global dynamics, or excitatory–inhibitory balance, missing higher-order directed organization such as cliques bound into cavities.
ocar.action: Reimann, Nolte, Scolamiero, Turner, Perin, Chindemi, Dłotko, Levi, Hess, and Markram, in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2017), construct directed graphs that follow information flow in a reconstructed neocortical microcircuit and analyze them with algebraic topology.
ocar.resolution: The synaptic network contains an abundance of neuronal cliques bound into cavities that guide correlated activity. In response to stimuli, correlated activity binds synaptically connected neurons into functional cliques and cavities that evolve in a stereotypical sequence toward peak complexity. They propose that the brain processes stimuli by forming increasingly complex functional cliques and cavities.
ocar.future_work: The clique-and-cavity sequence is offered as a proposed processing principle. The extract’s methods describe transmission-response matrices on the Blue Brain microcircuit (typical windows 5 and 10 ms) and Welch tests; a dedicated limitations section and quantitative Betti-number results are not in this truncated extract. Acknowledgments note related C. elegans connectome analysis.

summaries.beginner: Looking at cortex as one-way streets instead of undirected wires reveals clumps of fully connected cells wrapped around holes. This paper argues those growing clumps and holes are how the network organizes activity after a stimulus.
summaries.intermediate: Reimann and colleagues (Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience, published 2017; catalog year 2016) apply algebraic topology to directed synaptic graphs of a local neocortical network reconstructed by the Blue Brain Project. Accounting for transmission direction, they describe abundant cliques of neurons bound into cavities that shape correlated activity. Stimuli elicit a stereotyped sequence of increasingly complex functional cliques and cavities, which they propose as a missing structure–function link. Methods in the extract define transmission-response matrices from closely timed pre- and postsynaptic spikes.
summaries.advanced: The supplied extract is head-and-tail of the Frontiers article (abstract, introduction, and methods/acknowledgments), not the full results. Do not invent Betti numbers, clique counts, or simulation sizes that are not in this text. Keywords include directed networks, correlations, and Betti numbers; the C. elegans mention is an acknowledgment, not a reported main result. Catalog year is 2016; the PDF is dated published 12 June 2017.

plain_language_summary: Looking at cortex as one-way streets instead of undirected wires reveals clumps of fully connected cells wrapped around holes. This paper argues those growing clumps and holes are how the network organizes activity after a stimulus.

ocar.opportunity: A mesoscale whole-brain axonal projection atlas of the mouse is only as useful as the informatics that put raw injections into a common 3D space and turn signal into quantitative connection strengths.
ocar.challenge: Meaningful comparison of connectome data depends on a high-fidelity atlas template, precise mapping of raw datasets, accurate signal detection, quantitative strength algorithms, and an integrated public interface.
ocar.action: Kuan, Li, Lau, Feng, Bernard, Sunkin, Zeng, Dang, Hawrylycz, and Ng, in Methods (2015), describe key informatics pipeline steps behind the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas of the C57Bl/6J mouse.
ocar.resolution: The abstract presents a standardized platform that maps anatomical trajectories into a common 3D space, yielding a quantitative database of inter-areal and cell-type-specific projections with brain-wide coverage, a single data format, and open access at connectivity.brain-map.org, plus basic application use cases.
ocar.future_work: How later pipeline revisions changed quantification is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas is a public 3D map of which mouse brain areas send axons where. This methods paper explains the computer pipeline that turns injection images into that quantitative atlas.
summaries.intermediate: Kuan and colleagues (Methods, 2015) describe informatics for the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas, a mesoscale axonal-projection resource for the C57Bl/6J mouse. Trajectories are mapped into a common 3D template to produce a quantitative, cell-type-aware projection database with brain-wide coverage and a public interface (http://connectivity.brain-map.org/). The paper’s stated focus is pipeline steps—template, registration, signal detection, strength quantification, and online presentation—plus basic use cases.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Algorithm details, registration accuracy, and validation metrics are not in the abstract. Independent reading of the 2015 Methods article is required for pipeline internals.

plain_language_summary: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas is a public 3D map of which mouse brain areas send axons where. This methods paper explains the computer pipeline that turns injection images into that quantitative atlas.

ocar.opportunity: The word connectome is new, but maps of neural connections are old. Placing modern imaging in that history clarifies what is actually novel.
ocar.challenge: Contemporary definitions still rest on neuron theory from more than a century ago, and many current maps may be inaccurate surrogates of true anatomy.
ocar.action: Catani, Thiebaut de Schotten, Slater, and Dell’Acqua, in NeuroImage (2013), trace anatomical and physiological ideas behind modern connectome definitions.
ocar.resolution: The abstract argues that today’s advantage is quantitative imaging that can correlate structure, function, and behaviour, while still warning that a comprehensive human-brain connectome remains far off and that many maps are anatomically unfaithful.
ocar.future_work: How later large-scale projects changed that historical verdict is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: People have been drawing maps of brain connections for centuries. This history essay says modern imaging is powerful, but a true complete map of the human brain is still a long way off, and many of today’s pictures are only rough stand-ins.
summaries.intermediate: Catani, Thiebaut de Schotten, Slater, and Dell’Acqua (NeuroImage, 2013) review ‘proto-connectome’ maps and the conceptual origins of the modern term. They credit current methods with quantitative, multi-modal connectivity measures, while arguing that many contemporary maps remain inaccurate anatomical surrogates and that a comprehensive human connectome is historically distant.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Named historical maps, figures, and a full bibliographic argument are not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: People have been drawing maps of brain connections for centuries. This history essay says modern imaging is powerful, but a true complete map of the human brain is still a long way off, and many of today’s pictures are only rough stand-ins.

ocar.opportunity: Principles of cortical microcircuit connectivity have been inferred mostly from rodents. Direct human layer 2–3 measurements would show whether those rules transfer to an evolutionarily expanded cortex.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether human temporal-cortex pyramids show rodent-like reciprocity, strength–probability coupling, and cyclic motifs.
ocar.action: Peng, Bjelde, Aceituno, Geiger, and colleagues, in Science (2024), analyze multineuron patch-clamp recordings from layer 2–3 pyramidal neurons in human temporal cortex obtained during surgery, and compare network properties with rodents.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that human connectivity is heterogeneous, reciprocity is random, synaptic strength is independent of connection probability, and the graph is directed and mostly acyclic. Putting those principles into neural-network models increased dimensionality and improved performance on functionally relevant tasks.
ocar.future_work: How widely the directed-acyclic motif holds outside supragranular temporal cortex is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Most of what we know about how cortical cells wire to their neighbors comes from rodents. Recordings from human surgical tissue suggest a different pattern: connections run mostly one way, with few loops, which models say may help the network compute in higher dimensions.
summaries.intermediate: Peng et al. (Science, 2024) study human layer 2–3 temporal-cortex microcircuits with multi-neuron patch clamp on surgical samples. Per the catalog abstract and editor’s summary, unlike rodents, connectivity is heterogeneous, reciprocity is random, strength does not follow connection probability, and topology is directed and mostly acyclic. Implementing those rules in models increased dimensionality and task performance.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Patient count, connection probabilities, and the exact rodent comparison statistics are not in the abstract. The editor’s summary is catalog text, not a PDF extract.

plain_language_summary: Most of what we know about how cortical cells wire to their neighbors comes from rodents. Recordings from human surgical tissue suggest a different pattern: connections run mostly one way, with few loops, which models say may help the network compute in higher dimensions.

ocar.opportunity: Animals continuously choose the next action in the real world, but lab decision neuroscience has mostly used artificial trials. Genetic tools and connectomes now make naturalistic choice experimentally tractable in small nervous systems.
ocar.challenge: Trial-structured tasks may miss the neural logic of ongoing, innate decisions such as defensive choices.
ocar.action: Asinof and Card, in Annual Review of Neuroscience (2024), propose ‘reverse neuroethology’: pick experimentally accessible animals and use connectomes and genetic reagents to follow information flow during naturalistic choice, illustrated with Drosophila defensive behaviors.
ocar.resolution: The abstract presents this strategy as a way to study innate, rapid decision making, focusing on defensive behavioral choices in Drosophila melanogaster.
ocar.future_work: How far the framework extends beyond fly defense is left as a program for the field.

summaries.beginner: Lab studies of decisions often use unnatural trials, while real animals keep choosing what to do next in a messy world. This review proposes studying those natural choices in genetically tractable animals such as flies, using connectomes as a map.
summaries.intermediate: Asinof and Card (Annual Review of Neuroscience, 2024) propose reverse neuroethology: choose animal models for experimental access, then use connectomes and genetically encoded tools to analyze information flow during naturalistic choices. They focus on innate, rapid decisions, especially defensive behaviors in Drosophila melanogaster.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Specific circuits, figures, and a full literature synthesis are not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Lab studies of decisions often use unnatural trials, while real animals keep choosing what to do next in a messy world. This review proposes studying those natural choices in genetically tractable animals such as flies, using connectomes as a map.

ocar.opportunity: Osmium tetroxide is the workhorse lipid stain for biological EM, including synapse-resolution brain imaging. Knowing which osmium species actually generates contrast would guide better staining protocols.
ocar.challenge: Oxidation state and bonding of osmium in membranes, and why staining improves conductivity and reduces charging, remained open. Protocol development had relied on exhaustive search rather than rational design, and historical accounts emphasized osmate esters on unsaturated fatty-acid tails.
ocar.action: Li, Wildenberg, Boergens, Yang, Weber, Rieger, Arcidiacono, Klie, Kasthuri, and King, in ChemBioChem (2024), use photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM)—after PEEM imaging of mouse brain at synaptic resolution—to determine the nanoscale electronic structure of Os-stained biological samples.
ocar.resolution: Os(IV), as OsO2, forms nanoaggregates in lipid membranes, producing strong spatial variation in electronic structure. OsO2 is metallic, increasing the density of states near the Fermi level and thereby enhancing EM signal and specimen conductivity.
ocar.future_work: Identifying the contrast species is presented as opening rational staining-protocol development for high-resolution, high-contrast EM, including better uptake in large samples, better contrast, and chemistries that do not require highly toxic OsO4.

summaries.beginner: Brain tissue is stained with osmium so electron microscopes can see membranes. This chemistry paper reports that the dark contrast comes from metallic osmium dioxide specks in the lipids, which also help the sample conduct electrons.
summaries.intermediate: Li, Kasthuri, King and colleagues (ChemBioChem, 2024) follow PEEM imaging of mouse brain at synaptic resolution by mapping the electronic structure of osmium-stained tissue. They identify Os(IV) as OsO2 nanoaggregates in lipid membranes, with a metallic density of states near the Fermi level that boosts EM contrast and conductivity. The introduction contrasts this assignment with the usual ‘heavy metal / high Z’ story and with historical osmate-ester accounts, arguing that unknown speciation had blocked rational protocol design.
summaries.advanced: The extract is front matter plus the start of the introduction and a references tail; spectra, binding-energy values, and sample-prep recipes are not in this text. Do not invent peak energies or staining concentrations. Catalog author spellings differ slightly from the PDF (e.g. Narayanan Kasthuri). Version of record is ChemBioChem 2024, 25, e202400311.

plain_language_summary: Brain tissue is stained with osmium so electron microscopes can see membranes. This chemistry paper reports that the dark contrast comes from metallic osmium dioxide specks in the lipids, which also help the sample conduct electrons.

ocar.opportunity: A connectional map of adult zebrafish pallial zones would show whether this everted cortex is a set of dedicated modules or a highly mixed network, and would complement developmental neurogenetics.
ocar.challenge: Pallial areas are distinguished by topography, cytoarchitecture, immunohistochemistry, and genes, but their mutual and extrapallial connections were incompletely surveyed, and teleost pallia are diverse.
ocar.action: Yáñez, Folgueira, Lamas, and Anadón, in The Journal of Comparative Neurology (2021), use carbocyanine dye tracing and ancillary anatomy on the adult zebrafish dorsal telencephalon (D).
ocar.resolution: Interconnectivity among major pallial zones is poor, especially between medial (Dm), lateral/dorsal (Dl, Dd), and posterior (Dp) regions, suggesting dedicated modules. Extrapallial connections are also compartmental: major extratelencephalic afferents include preglomerular nuclei (to Dl, Dd, Dm), posterior tuberal nucleus (to Dm), and lateral recess nucleus (to Dl); subpallial Vv, Vd, and Vs mainly innervate Dl/Dd and Dp. Efferents are region-specific (e.g. rostral Dm to dorsal entopeduncular nucleus; Dp with olfactory bulbs; Dc from Dl–Dd toward pretectum and tectum).
ocar.future_work: The abstract compares the zebrafish pallial connectome with other teleosts and notes usefulness for early-stage neurogenetic studies; functional mapping of the modules is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: The roof of the adult zebrafish forebrain is divided into several neighborhoods. This tracing study finds those neighborhoods are only weakly wired to each other, as if they were separate workstations.
summaries.intermediate: Yáñez, Folgueira, Lamas, and Anadón (Journal of Comparative Neurology, 2021) map adult zebrafish pallium with carbocyanine dyes. Interconnectivity among pallial divisions is poor, particularly linking medial, lateral/dorsal, and posterior zones. Extrapallial afferents are similarly compartmental (preglomerular, posterior tuberal, lateral recess), subpallial homologues of striatum/amygdala/pallidum mainly target Dl/Dd and Dp, and each pallial region has characteristic outputs, including a central zone projecting toward pretectum and optic tectum.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Tracer n, injection sites, and photomicrographs are not in the abstract. Homology claims for Vv, Vd, and Vs are the authors’ anatomical framing, not independently verified here.

plain_language_summary: The roof of the adult zebrafish forebrain is divided into several neighborhoods. This tracing study finds those neighborhoods are only weakly wired to each other, as if they were separate workstations.

ocar.opportunity: Relating the magnitude and structure of interneuronal correlations to synaptic connectivity is a core problem for interpreting population recordings together with wiring.
ocar.challenge: Balanced-network theory of the asynchronous state assumed uncorrelated feedforward spike trains, so input correlations arose only from overlapping projections. Real feedforward input from thalamus, other areas, or other layers can itself be correlated, and standard linear-response/diffusion approximations assume sparse or weak connectivity and uncorrelated Gaussian white noise.
ocar.action: Baker, Ebsch, Lampl, and Rosenbaum, in Physical Review E (2019), extend densely connected balanced-network theory to correlated feedforward spike trains and analyze the resulting correlated state, comparing it with cancellation that keeps asynchronous-state correlations weak as network size grows.
ocar.resolution: Correlated feedforward input produces much larger downstream correlations than the classical asynchronous state. Unlike that state, the correlated state yields a tight excitatory–inhibitory balance consistent with in vivo cortical recordings. In the asynchronous analysis, O(1) sources of input covariance cancel so that total input and spike-count covariance vanish with network size N.
ocar.future_work: The extract notes that Fokker–Planck diffusion approximations are not justified for this densely connected model (Discussion is cited but truncated). The implied use is interpreting cortical correlation structure when feedforward spikes are themselves correlated.

summaries.beginner: Brain models often assume incoming spike trains are independent, which keeps cortical cells nearly uncorrelated. This theory paper says that if those inputs are themselves correlated, the whole network enters a much more correlated state.
summaries.intermediate: Baker, Ebsch, Lampl, and Rosenbaum (Physical Review E, 2019; extract is a bioRxiv version of the same study) analyze balanced networks driven by correlated feedforward input. Prior asynchronous-state theory kept average spike correlations weak via cancellation even when some pairs could be stronger under special connectivity. With correlated upstream spike trains, the recurrent network produces much larger correlations—a correlated state—with tight E–I balance matching in vivo observations. The extract derives spike-train cross-spectra for the asynchronous case and tests terms of that relation in simulations without relying on a diffusion approximation.
summaries.advanced: The extract is a truncated bioRxiv PDF (posted 18 March 2019) rather than the typeset PRE article; equation numbers and figure panels in the tail are incomplete. Do not invent correlation coefficients, N, or firing-rate values beyond the O(1) versus O(1/N) scaling stated in the text. Catalog title uses the plural ‘states’; the preprint title uses the singular.

plain_language_summary: Brain models often assume incoming spike trains are independent, which keeps cortical cells nearly uncorrelated. This theory paper says that if those inputs are themselves correlated, the whole network enters a much more correlated state.

ocar.opportunity: A classified human brain connectome that combines anatomy with neurophysiology would help relate structure to function and to clinical mapping of neuropsychiatric disorders.
ocar.challenge: Many connectivity methods exist across EEG, MEG, non-invasive stimulation, structural and functional MRI, and graph measures of local and global connectivity, and they are not automatically commensurate.
ocar.action: Rossini, Iorio, Bentivoglio, Bertini, Ferreri, Gerloff, Ilmoniemi, Miraglia, Nitsche, Pestilli, Rosanova, Shirota, Tesoriero, Ugawa, Vecchio, Ziemann, and Hallett, in Clinical Neurophysiology (2019), review IFCN-relevant methods for studying the human connectome with emphasis on neurophysiological techniques, following an IFCN-endorsed meeting.
ocar.resolution: The abstract describes a multimodality program to identify networks with neurobiologically meaningful, computable measures, integrating neurophysiology with flow/metabolic neuroimaging so that anatomical and functional connections can be placed on one map for structure–function and etiological interpretation.
ocar.future_work: Specific method-by-method recommendations beyond the abstract’s scope are not given here.

summaries.beginner: Doctors and scientists map human brain networks with electrical recordings, magnetic stimulation, and scanners. This IFCN review surveys those tools and how to combine them.
summaries.intermediate: Rossini and colleagues (Clinical Neurophysiology, 2019) review methods for the human connectome with a neurophysiology focus, in an IFCN-sponsored paper. The aim is to classify networks with computable measures and to integrate physiological mapping (EEG, MEG, non-invasive stimulation) with structural and functional MRI of flow and metabolism, including local and global connectivity metrics.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Protocol recipes, recommended pipelines, and a full methods table are not in the abstract. Catalog authors list Ilmoniemi twice.

plain_language_summary: Doctors and scientists map human brain networks with electrical recordings, magnetic stimulation, and scanners. This IFCN review surveys those tools and how to combine them.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse anterior and midcingulate areas 24a/24b and 24a′/24b′ are implicated in cognition, emotion, and pain; a complete afferent–efferent map would give an anatomical basis for those functions.
ocar.challenge: Afferents of these areas had been described, but efferents needed a matching anterograde-tracing survey to finish the cingulate connectome and to compare ACC versus MCC and dorsal versus ventral subdivisions.
ocar.action: Fillinger, Yalcin, Barrot, and Veinante, in Brain Structure and Function (2017), inject anterograde tracers into mouse areas 24a/24b (ACC) and 24a′/24b′ (MCC) and chart cortical and subcortical projections.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports a shared projection pattern to cortex (intracingulate, retrosplenial, parietal associative), basal forebrain, hypothalamus, thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord, with denser ACC than MCC output and topographic differences between dorsal (24b/24b′) and ventral (24a/24a′) areas, suggesting shared plus area-specific roles.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the maps as the anatomical basis needed to address ACC/MCC function; causal tests are not claimed there.

summaries.beginner: This paper traces outgoing wires from mouse cingulate cortex and reports that neighboring cingulate patches share many targets but differ in how strongly and exactly they project.
summaries.intermediate: Fillinger, Yalcin, Barrot, and Veinante (Brain Structure and Function, 2017) complete a mouse cingulate connectome by mapping efferents of ACC areas 24a/24b and MCC areas 24a′/24b′. Common targets include intracortical, basal-forebrain, hypothalamic, thalamic, brainstem, and spinal structures. ACC projections are overall denser than MCC, with further dorsal–ventral topography, supporting shared plus specialized functions.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Injection n, density scoring, and the companion afferent paper’s details are not in this abstract.

plain_language_summary: This paper traces outgoing wires from mouse cingulate cortex and reports that neighboring cingulate patches share many targets but differ in how strongly and exactly they project.

ocar.opportunity: Super-resolution fluorescence deep in tissue would let synaptic circuits be mapped optically if scattering and spherical aberration can be controlled.
ocar.challenge: Standard mounting mismatches the refractive index of immersion oil (1.518), limiting super-resolution depth.
ocar.action: Ke, Nakai, Fujimoto, Takayama, Yoshida, Kitajima, Sato, and Imai, in Cell Reports (2016), introduce SeeDB2, an index-optimized clearing agent matched to oil immersion, and apply volumetric super-resolution imaging to mouse neurons and fly medulla.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports preservation of fine morphology and fluorescent proteins, super-resolution to depths >100 μm (an order of magnitude deeper than standard mounting), accumulation of inhibitory synapses on spine heads in NMDA-receptor-deficient neurons, and unexpected heterogeneity of Mi1 axon-bouton orientations in the fly motion circuit.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents volumetric super-resolution of cleared tissue as a strategy for synaptic-level connectomics; EM-level completeness is not claimed there.

summaries.beginner: Seeing synapses with a light microscope deep inside tissue is usually blurry. This paper introduces a clearing recipe that matches oil-immersion lenses so super-resolution can go more than ten times deeper.
summaries.intermediate: Ke and colleagues (Cell Reports, 2016) develop SeeDB2 to match fixed-tissue refractive index to immersion oil (1.518). They report super-resolution imaging >100 μm deep with preserved morphology and fluorescent proteins, extra inhibitory synapses on spine heads in NMDA-receptor-deficient neurons, and heterogeneous Mi1 bouton orientations in Drosophila medulla. The work is positioned as optical connectomics at synaptic scale.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Depth (>100 μm), synapse counts, and Mi1 orientation statistics were not verified beyond the abstract’s qualitative claims.

plain_language_summary: Seeing synapses with a light microscope deep inside tissue is usually blurry. This paper introduces a clearing recipe that matches oil-immersion lenses so super-resolution can go more than ten times deeper.

ocar.opportunity: Focal epilepsies increasingly look like network diseases, so individual connectomes assessed with graph theory could become diagnostic and treatment biomarkers.
ocar.challenge: Translational measurement of abnormal networks had been limited by methods; connectomics now offers person-specific maps but produces complex big data.
ocar.action: Gleichgerrcht, Kocher, and Bonilha, in Epilepsia (2015), review emerging connectomics evidence on architecture, dynamics, and function in epilepsy and discuss links to conceptual models and personalized care.
ocar.resolution: The abstract argues that graph analysis of the personal connectome can reveal organization prone to abnormal dynamics and epileptogenesis, that a rapidly growing evidence base already addresses fundamental aspects of epileptic networks, and that unique per-subject network information may help explain outcome variability.
ocar.future_work: The abstract stresses the need for collaborative, rigorous evaluation of connectomic big data to realize personalized medicine; no single new cohort is reported there.

summaries.beginner: Epilepsy often involves whole-brain networks, not just one damaged spot. This review explains how mapping a person’s brain connections with network math might eventually guide diagnosis and treatment.
summaries.intermediate: Gleichgerrcht, Kocher, and Bonilha (Epilepsia, 2015) review MRI/connectomic and graph-theoretic studies of epilepsy. They argue that network endophenotypes could be biomarkers, that connectomics can test hypotheses from basic models of epileptogenesis, and that individual connectomes may inform variable surgical or medical outcomes. They call for collaborative analysis of rich per-subject data.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No graph-theory metrics, cohort sizes, or a study-count table appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Epilepsy often involves whole-brain networks, not just one damaged spot. This review explains how mapping a person’s brain connections with network math might eventually guide diagnosis and treatment.

ocar.opportunity: Excitatory afferents onto cerebellar Purkinje cells occupy stereotyped, non-overlapping synaptic territories; a secreted ligand–receptor pair could explain that patterning.
ocar.challenge: What sets synapse number, morphology, and subcellular localization for parallel-fiber versus climbing-fiber inputs was unclear.
ocar.action: Sigoillot, Iyer, Binda, González-Calvo, Talleur, Vodjdani, Isope, and Selimi, in Cell Reports (2015), study the complement C1Q-related protein C1QL1 and its receptor BAI3 in mouse cerebellum.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that BAI3 modulates synaptogenesis of both parallel-fiber and climbing-fiber afferents, while timely, restricted C1QL1 expression in inferior olivary neurons assigns climbing-fiber territory. Given broad C1QL/BAI expression, they propose a general mechanism for building functional connectivity.
ocar.future_work: Generality beyond cerebellum is inferred from expression, not demonstrated in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Two kinds of excitatory input land on cerebellar Purkinje cells in tidy, separate zones. This paper identifies a secreted protein and its receptor that help set those territories.
summaries.intermediate: Sigoillot and colleagues (Cell Reports, 2015) show that C1QL1 and its adhesion-GPCR receptor BAI3 control excitatory connectivity onto Purkinje cells. BAI3 affects both parallel-fiber and climbing-fiber synaptogenesis; olivary C1QL1 expression timing and restriction position climbing fibers. Broad C1QL/BAI expression is taken to suggest a general wiring mechanism.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Synapse counts, knockout phenotypes, and olivary expression timing are not quantified in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Two kinds of excitatory input land on cerebellar Purkinje cells in tidy, separate zones. This paper identifies a secreted protein and its receptor that help set those territories.

ocar.opportunity: Human connectome research has been paced by visualization innovations, from diffusion glyphs to tract renderings to graph views of functional connectivity.
ocar.challenge: Unresolved tensions remain: probabilistic versus deterministic tractography’s visual appeal, multimodal reduction, clutter when rendering a full connectome in anatomical space, and trade-offs among anatomy versus topology, aesthetics versus information, and thoroughness versus readability.
ocar.action: Margulies, Böttger, Watanabe, and Gorgolewski, in NeuroImage (2013), review visualization methods for anatomical and functional connectivity, survey interactive research tools, and discuss concerns in presenting connectivity results.
ocar.resolution: The abstract frames visualization as enabling intuitive insight while documenting persistent problems and the need to negotiate those design tensions.
ocar.future_work: The abstract points to ongoing development of interactive tools and to unresolved presentation issues rather than a single software release.

summaries.beginner: Maps of human brain connections are only as useful as the pictures that show them. This review walks through how those pictures evolved and why they still get cluttered or misleading.
summaries.intermediate: Margulies, Böttger, Watanabe, and Gorgolewski (NeuroImage, 2013) survey visualization of the human connectome: tensor glyphs, anatomical tract rendering, and graph-based functional connectivity. They discuss unresolved problems (probabilistic tractography’s weaker visual appeal, multimodal reduction, anatomical clutter) and tensions between anatomic versus connectomic emphasis, aesthetics versus information, and completeness versus readability, plus available interactive tools.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Named visualization tools and screenshots from the NeuroImage paper are not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Maps of human brain connections are only as useful as the pictures that show them. This review walks through how those pictures evolved and why they still get cluttered or misleading.

ocar.opportunity: Intrinsically photosensitive melanopsin ganglion cells sit in retinal circuits fed by rods and cones, so mapping their morphology and synapses would clarify how irradiance signals are combined with image-forming input.
ocar.challenge: That circuitry was poorly understood, including whether inner- and outer-stratifying melanopsin cells are independent populations and what bipolar versus amacrine input they receive.
ocar.action: Jusuf, Lee, Hannibal, and Grünert, in the European Journal of Neuroscience (2007), study melanopsin-containing ganglion cells in common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) with morphology, tiling, and synaptic markers (CtBP2 for presumed bipolar synapses; gephyrin for presumed amacrine synapses).
ocar.resolution: Outer-stratifying dendrites tile with little overlap, whereas they largely overlap inner-stratifying fields, suggesting independent populations. Both types show colocalized puncta for both markers across the dendritic tree. CtBP2 density on inner dendrites was about 50% higher than on outer dendrites; gephyrin density was comparable between strata but higher than CtBP2. Inner-stratifying cells may receive input from diffuse bipolar DB6.
ocar.future_work: The abstract frames the pattern as consistent with bipolar and amacrine input across the tree; it does not report functional recordings.

summaries.beginner: Some primate retinal cells contain the pigment melanopsin and also receive ordinary photoreceptor input. This study maps those cells in marmoset and counts likely synapses on their inner versus outer dendrites.
summaries.intermediate: In the European Journal of Neuroscience (2007), Jusuf, Lee, Hannibal, and Grünert characterize melanopsin ganglion cells in marmoset. Outer-stratifying cells tile; inner- and outer-stratifying fields overlap. Using CtBP2 and gephyrin puncta, both populations appear to receive bipolar and amacrine input across the dendritic tree, with CtBP2 density about 50% higher on inner dendrites. Inner-stratifying cells are suggested to receive DB6 bipolar input.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No tiling statistics beyond the qualitative overlap claim, and no absolute puncta densities, appear in the abstract. The ~50% CtBP2 inner-versus-outer difference is the only numeric comparison given.

plain_language_summary: Some primate retinal cells contain the pigment melanopsin and also receive ordinary photoreceptor input. This study maps those cells in marmoset and counts likely synapses on their inner versus outer dendrites.

ocar.opportunity: Thalamic neuromodulation is increasingly used for drug-resistant epilepsy; neuroimaging of thalamic structure, nuclei, and networks could improve targeting and outcome prediction.
ocar.challenge: The thalamus is altered in common epilepsy syndromes, traditional stereotactic coordinates may miss patient-specific nuclei, and stimulation effects on networks are incompletely characterized.
ocar.action: Middlebrooks, He, Grewal, and Keller, in Epilepsy Research (2022), review neuroimaging and thalamic connectomics in epilepsy neuromodulation: thalamic changes as rationale, methods for imaging nuclei and the case for direct surgical targeting, and neuroimaging as a potential biomarker of stimulation effects and outcomes.
ocar.resolution: The review argues for imaging-defined targeting rather than reliance on traditional stereotactic coordinates alone, and for using neuroimaging to assess how thalamic stimulation alters networks and to serve as an outcome biomarker.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents these as roles neuroimaging could play; it does not report a new trial.

summaries.beginner: Stimulating the thalamus can help some people whose seizures do not respond to drugs. This review discusses how brain scans of thalamic connections might guide where to place those stimulators.
summaries.intermediate: In Epilepsy Research (2022), Middlebrooks, He, Grewal, and Keller review neuroimaging and thalamic connectomics for neuromodulation in drug-resistant epilepsy. They cover structural and functional thalamic changes as rationale, methods to image distinct nuclei and why direct targeting may beat atlas coordinates, and the potential of imaging to track stimulation effects and outcomes.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No sample sizes, seizure-reduction percentages, or named trials appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Stimulating the thalamus can help some people whose seizures do not respond to drugs. This review discusses how brain scans of thalamic connections might guide where to place those stimulators.

ocar.opportunity: Deep brain stimulation can help severe obsessive-compulsive disorder, but connecting stimulation sites to distributed networks rather than a single nucleus could explain clinical benefit and unify cortical and subcortical interventions.
ocar.challenge: Best anatomical targets and mechanisms remain ambiguous, limiting routine clinical use even when DBS is considered effective.
ocar.action: Baldermann, Schüller, Kohl, Voon, Li, Hollunder, Figee, Haber, Sheth, Mosley, Huys, Johnson, Butson, Ackermans, Bouwens van der Vlis, Leentjens, Barbe, Visser-Vandewalle, Kuhn, and Horn, in Biological Psychiatry (2021), critically review connectomic DBS for OCD, integrating connectivity analyses with neuromodulation to characterize a network whose modulation reduces obsessions and compulsions.
ocar.resolution: They argue that broader network changes, not only local impact at the electrode, account for improvement, scrutinize conflicting findings to merge common and diverse pathways, and propose a unified network that, when modulated cortically or subcortically, alleviates OCD symptoms.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents a synthesized target network rather than a prospective trial of that map.

summaries.beginner: Brain stimulation for severe OCD may work by hitting a whole circuit, not one tiny spot. This review tries to draw that circuit from imaging and stimulation studies.
summaries.intermediate: In Biological Psychiatry (2021), Baldermann, Horn and colleagues review connectomic deep brain stimulation for obsessive-compulsive disorder. They argue that distributed network effects better explain symptom relief than local stimulation alone, reconcile apparently conflicting target findings, and propose a unified network for cortical or subcortical neuromodulation.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No electrode coordinates, tractography atlases, or outcome percentages appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Brain stimulation for severe OCD may work by hitting a whole circuit, not one tiny spot. This review tries to draw that circuit from imaging and stimulation studies.

ocar.opportunity: Undergraduate neuroscience majors who can handle data-science and graph-theoretic tools would be able to read contemporary systems and connectomics literature rather than remaining on a calculus-plus-parametric-statistics diet.
ocar.challenge: Credit-hour pressure, outdated statistics requirements, and faculty whose quantitative skills have atrophied leave students ill-equipped for big-data neuroscience, including connectomics framed as 21st-century functional neuroanatomy.
ocar.action: Hoy, in Neuroscience Letters (2021), comments on quantitative skills in undergraduate neuroscience education, arguing for data-science coursework of the kind required in social sciences and for short-format workshops, journal clubs, and independent studies in which students and instructors learn together, using neuroscience-contextualized materials.
ocar.resolution: The commentary holds that additional training in mathematics, statistics, computer science, and/or data science is urgently needed even to understand current literature, and that faculty awareness of the gap can be ameliorated (not solved) by co-learning formats and web teaching clips.
ocar.future_work: Curriculum reform at scale is urged; the piece does not report an implemented course evaluation.

summaries.beginner: Neuroscience students still take old-style math while the field now runs on huge datasets and network graphs. This commentary says they need data-science training, even if faculty have to learn alongside them.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroscience Letters (2021), R. Hoy comments that the traditional year of calculus plus a semester of parametric statistics does not prepare undergraduate neuroscience majors for big-data and systems work, including connectomics. Students are credit-squeezed; faculty may feel their quantitative skills have faded. Hoy recommends data-science courses used in social sciences and co-learning workshops/journal clubs with neuroscience-contextualized quantitative teaching.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No enrollment statistics or controlled education outcomes appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Neuroscience students still take old-style math while the field now runs on huge datasets and network graphs. This commentary says they need data-science training, even if faculty have to learn alongside them.

ocar.opportunity: Birds achieve complex cognition without a six-layered cortex; comparing hippocampal connectivity and adult neurogenesis along the anterior–posterior axis could inform hippocampal evolution.
ocar.challenge: Early comparative anatomy misread the avian telencephalon as a hypertrophied striatum; even with a pallial consensus, species-specific hippocampal morphology still complicates homology with mammals.
ocar.action: Herold, Schlömer, Mafoppa-Fomat, Mehlhorn, Amunts, and Axer, in Cortex (2019), use 3D polarized light imaging (3D-PLI) on the pigeon hippocampal formation (HF) and assess adult neurogenesis across HF subdivisions and caudal regions.
ocar.resolution: Pigeon HF, like mammalian HF, shows regional specializations of connectivity along the anterior–posterior axis, plus different levels of adult neurogenesis in subdivisions and in the most caudal regions, pointing to functional specialization along that axis. The authors conclude that morphologies are species-specific but hippocampal characteristics of connectivity, cells, and adult neurogenesis remain conserved relative to mammals.
ocar.future_work: The abstract offers new aspects for ongoing debates on hippocampal evolution and mind, without claiming a completed homology table.

summaries.beginner: Bird brains do not look like mammal brains, but their hippocampus still has specialized wiring along its length. This pigeon imaging study adds that pattern to the evolutionary comparison.
summaries.intermediate: In Cortex (2019), Herold, Amunts, Axer and colleagues apply 3D polarized light imaging to pigeon hippocampal formation and report anterior–posterior specialization of connectivity, together with subdivision- and caudal-dependent adult neurogenesis. They argue for conserved hippocampal traits of connectivity, cells, and neurogenesis despite species-specific morphology.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No 3D-PLI anisotropy values or neurogenesis cell counts appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Bird brains do not look like mammal brains, but their hippocampus still has specialized wiring along its length. This pigeon imaging study adds that pattern to the evolutionary comparison.

ocar.opportunity: A focused comparison of primate connectomes, rather than all animals at once, could show which long-range connections are shared and which are human- or species-specific adaptations.
ocar.challenge: Long-range connections improve communication but are costly; methods (white-matter volume, histology, tracers, dMRI tractography, functional MRI) disagree, and cortical homologies plus false-positive tractography remain obstacles.
ocar.action: Rilling and van den Heuvel, in Brain, Behavior and Evolution (2018), review comparative primate connectomics across structural and resting-state measures, including humans, chimpanzees, and rhesus macaques, and outline how to expand species coverage with postmortem diffusion tractography.
ocar.resolution: Larger primate brains appear less well connected globally than smaller ones, yet humans have more connections than expected for cortical neuron number, possibly concentrated in prefrontal cortex. Human-specific structural and functional connections are reported in language, imitation, tool-use, and (for functional connectivity) empathy-related cortex, against a background of widespread overlap with nonhuman primates.
ocar.future_work: They urge postmortem dMRI to include more species, careful homology, better tractography to limit false positives/negatives, and linking connectivity variation to behavior within and across species.

summaries.beginner: This review compares wiring maps among primates and asks what is unusual about human long-range connections, especially in language and tool-use areas.
summaries.intermediate: In Brain, Behavior and Evolution (2018), Rilling and van den Heuvel review comparative primate connectomics. They synthesize white-matter, tracing, dMRI, and functional-connectivity evidence: larger primate brains are less globally connected, but humans may exceed expectations given cortical neuron number (possibly prefrontal). Overlap with macaques/chimpanzees is broad, with human-specific links in language, imitation, tool use, and empathy-related functional connections. They recommend expanding postmortem tractography beyond the usual three species.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No quantitative edge-overlap percentages or tractography error rates appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: This review compares wiring maps among primates and asks what is unusual about human long-range connections, especially in language and tool-use areas.

ocar.opportunity: Major depressive disorder involves several large-scale functional networks, so resting-state connectivity could supply a systems-level picture of the illness.
ocar.challenge: Seed-based and ICA studies of depression do not all agree, and findings need to be placed inside existing hypotheses of network dysfunction rather than listed as isolated edges.
ocar.action: Mulders, van Eijndhoven, Schene, Beckmann, and Tendolkar, in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews (2015), review resting-state functional connectivity studies of MDD that used seed-based correlation or independent component analysis.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports four relatively consistent patterns: increased connectivity within the anterior default mode network; increased connectivity between the salience network and the anterior default mode network; altered connectivity between anterior and posterior default mode network; and decreased connectivity between the posterior default mode network and the central executive network. The authors treat depression as a network-based disorder.
ocar.future_work: How these four motifs should be tested prospectively, and how much study-level heterogeneity remains, cannot be read from the abstract alone.

summaries.beginner: Depression is not only a chemical story; it also shows up as changed conversations among large brain networks at rest. This review gathers those imaging studies and highlights a few patterns that keep appearing.
summaries.intermediate: Mulders, van Eijndhoven, Schene, Beckmann, and Tendolkar (Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, 2015) review resting-state fMRI connectivity in major depressive disorder using seed-based correlation or ICA. Despite between-study differences, recurring findings are increased anterior default-mode connectivity, increased salience–anterior default-mode coupling, changed anterior–posterior default-mode coupling, and decreased posterior default-mode–central-executive coupling.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Study counts, seed choices, and effect sizes are not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Depression is not only a chemical story; it also shows up as changed conversations among large brain networks at rest. This review gathers those imaging studies and highlights a few patterns that keep appearing.

ocar.opportunity: Recovery after brain damage, and the ability to resect eloquent-looking cortex without lasting deficit, are hard to explain if adult function is strictly modular and static.
ocar.challenge: A localizationist map of fixed critical regions does not account for postoperative recovery or for remapping seen when the same patient is operated on more than once.
ocar.action: Duffau, in Cortex (2014), reviews serial mappings in patients who underwent awake surgery for diffuse glioma infiltrating eloquent structures.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports three strands: intraoperative cortical and subcortical electrical mapping that supports a network view of language and other functions; pre/post neuropsychological and functional imaging evidence that large resections of supposedly critical cortex can spare lasting sequelae via circuit reorganization; and remapping across repeated surgeries for tumor relapse. White-matter connectivity is presented as the main limit on that plastic potential.
ocar.future_work: A better connectomic account of which subcortical pathways are indispensable is the implied constraint on how far adult reorganization can go; details are outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Adult brains can reroute function after injury more than old modular maps suggest. This surgical review argues that glioma operations done awake show that plasticity, not a fixed list of “untouchable” spots, often keeps language and thought going—until key white-matter cables are cut.
summaries.intermediate: Duffau (Cortex, 2014) uses serial mappings from awake glioma surgery to argue against a static localizationist model of adult brain function. Intraoperative cortical and subcortical stimulation supports network-level organization (including language), combined neuropsychology and functional imaging show that large resections of “critical” cortex can avoid permanent sequelae through reorganization, and repeated operations document remapping in the same patients. The limiting factor emphasized is white-matter connectivity: extensive subcortical damage is what blocks recovery.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Case-series size, mapping protocols, and which tracts are treated as plastic limits are not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Adult brains can reroute function after injury more than old modular maps suggest. This surgical review argues that glioma operations done awake show that plasticity, not a fixed list of “untouchable” spots, often keeps language and thought going—until key white-matter cables are cut.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic and large-scale brain connectivity shape neural responses, represent the sensory world, coordinate distributed processing, and store a structural record of the past, which naturally suggests the mathematics of networks.
ocar.challenge: Network science had already transformed other fields, but its contributions to neuroimaging were still being organized; a historical map of the ideas was needed.
ocar.action: Sporns, in NeuroImage (2012), offers a personal perspective on the confluence of networks and neuroimaging.
ocar.resolution: The abstract presents the article as a chart of major intellectual themes at the meeting of graph theory and brain imaging, not as a new empirical connectome. Connectivity is treated as fundamental to brain function at multiple scales.
ocar.future_work: What themes the essay flags as unfinished cannot be recovered from the abstract alone.

summaries.beginner: Brain science borrowed the idea of networks from other fields so it could talk about wiring, not only about single regions. This essay looks back at how that way of thinking entered neuroimaging.
summaries.intermediate: Sporns (NeuroImage, 2012) writes a personal perspective on networks in neuroimaging. Connectivity is fundamental to how neurons respond, how the brain represents statistics of the world, how distributed resources are coordinated, and how structure retains a record of the past. Network science, already productive elsewhere, is described as beginning to contribute across neuroscience. The article charts origins of major intellectual themes rather than reporting a new dataset.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Which historical themes are emphasized, and any cited milestones, are not recoverable from the abstract alone.

plain_language_summary: Brain science borrowed the idea of networks from other fields so it could talk about wiring, not only about single regions. This essay looks back at how that way of thinking entered neuroimaging.

ocar.opportunity: If dendritic spines can form and disappear without rebuilding axonal and dendritic arbors, a neuron could switch among many wiring diagrams using only local geometry.
ocar.challenge: The size of that structural-plasticity repertoire is not obvious: it depends on how many nearby axons a dendrite could still connect to, relative to how many synapses it already has.
ocar.action: Stepanyants, Hof, and Chklovskii, in Neuron (2002), define the filling fraction as the ratio of synapses on a dendrite to axons passing within a spine length of that dendrite, and they estimate it from geometry and anatomical data.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports filling fractions of 0.26 in mouse neocortex and 0.22–0.34 in rat hippocampus, and an increase by a factor of 1.6–1.8 from macaque V1 to areas V2, V4, and 7a. Because the filling fraction is much smaller than 1, spine remodeling can contribute substantially to structural plasticity without major arbor remodeling.
ocar.future_work: Implications for learning rules and for comparing cortical areas further are outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: A dendrite is surrounded by many axons it could touch with a short spine, but it only makes synapses with some of them. This theory paper estimates that leftover “empty slots” are common, so rewiring spines could change circuits a lot without growing new branches.
summaries.intermediate: Stepanyants, Hof, and Chklovskii (Neuron, 2002) quantify how many distinct connectivity patterns are available if spines form and disappear without major arbor remodeling. That number depends on the filling fraction: synapses on a dendrite divided by axons within a spine length of it. They calculate filling fraction 0.26 in mouse neocortex and 0.22–0.34 in rat hippocampus, with a 1.6–1.8-fold increase from macaque V1 to V2, V4, and 7a. Because the ratio is well below 1, spine remodeling is argued to be a large reservoir of structural plasticity.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Filling-fraction values above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Geometrical derivations, species/area samples, and uncertainty on those ratios require the Neuron paper.

plain_language_summary: A dendrite is surrounded by many axons it could touch with a short spine, but it only makes synapses with some of them. This theory paper estimates that leftover “empty slots” are common, so rewiring spines could change circuits a lot without growing new branches.
